note: Only sources actually opened are in studies. Ratios are quoted verbatim; none computed. 'scope' marks NI versus UK/Ireland comparators. 'ownCommissioned' marks studies commissioned by the delivering organisation or its sector body.

studies.title: The cost of late intervention in Northern Ireland
studies.author: Peter Fitzsimons and William Teager (Early Intervention Foundation)
studies.commissioner: Early Intervention Transformation Programme (EITP) - NI Executive/Atlantic Philanthropies Delivering Social Change Signature Programme
studies.urlNote: EIF site now redirects (EIF became Foundations); the PDF was read from the Wayback Machine copy.
studies.programme: No single programme: cost to the public sector of late intervention for children and young people
studies.method: fiscal cost estimate (cost of late intervention / cost-avoidance baseline); not SROI, not CBA
studies.forecastOrEvaluation: neither - a cross-sectional estimate of current spend
studies.headlineVerbatim: The annual short-run cost to the public sector of late intervention in Northern Ireland is estimated at £536 million per year. This is equivalent to £288 for every Northern Ireland resident, or £1,166 per child.
studies.period: latest year's data, "generally reflecting activity in 2016/17"; all costs converted to 2017/18 prices
studies.financialProxies: Spend apportioned from budgets, or average cost per incidence x number of service users; full methodology in report appendix
studies.assurance: none stated; commissioned analysis by an independent What Works centre
studies.notes: Largest drivers per report: child protection and safeguarding, domestic violence, youth economic inactivity. This is a cost baseline, not a return on any programme. Widely re-cited (e.g. Barnardo's NI 2023, EITP infographic).

studies.title: A cluster randomised controlled trial and evaluation and cost-effectiveness analysis of the Roots of Empathy schools-based programme for improving social and emotional well-being outcomes among 8- to 9-year-olds in Northern Ireland
studies.author: Connolly P, Miller S, Kee F, Sloan S, Gildea A, McIntosh E, Boyer N, Bland M (Queen's University Belfast et al.)
studies.method: cost-utility analysis within a cluster RCT (independent academic economic evaluation); not SROI
studies.headlineVerbatim: The ICER was £9571 per QALY gained (95% CI –£87,776 to £106,676)
otherFiguresVerbatim: The incremental cost was £153 (95% CI £14 to £292), significantly higher for ROE ( p = 0.032).
The incremental QALY gain of 0.0160 (95% CI –0.0143 to 0.0462) was not statistically significant ( p = 0.300).
The study also found that ROE was likely to be cost-effective in line with national guidelines.
studies.period: time horizon 3.75 years (45 months); costs in 2014 GBP
outcomesValued: secondary: SDQ prosocial and total difficulties scores (ICER per unit)
studies.financialProxies: Public sector perspective; unit costs from PSSRU 2014 (GP £46, school nurse £63, social worker £41, educational psychologist £41, etc.) and NHS Reference Costs 2013/14 (A&E £72, psychiatrist £228)
studies.deadweight: not applicable - counterfactual is the randomised waiting-list control group
studies.dropOff: discounting at 1.5% (NICE public health rate); 3.5% as sensitivity analysis
studies.assurance: peer-reviewed NIHR journal; independent of programme provider
studies.notes: Threshold £20,000-30,000 per QALY. Probability cost-effective 83.1% at £20,000 (90.1% at £30,000) in base case per Table 29. QALY gain itself not significant.

studies.title: Proving the Power of Positive Parenting: A randomised controlled trial to investigate the effectiveness of the Incredible Years BASIC Parent training programme in an Irish Context (Short-term Outcomes)
studies.author: Sinéad McGilloway, Tracey Bywater, Grainne Ni Mhaille, Mairéad Furlong, Donal O'Neill, Catherine Comiskey, Yvonne Leckey, Paul Kelly and Michael Donnelly
studies.commissioner: Archways, with support from The Atlantic Philanthropies
studies.programme: Incredible Years BASIC parent programme (also delivered in NI)
studies.place: Republic of Ireland (Archways sites); co-author Michael Donnelly is at QUB
studies.scope: Ireland - comparable programme that also runs in NI
studies.method: cost-effectiveness analysis within RCT plus projected long-run net present value (cost-benefit style)
studies.forecastOrEvaluation: cost-effectiveness is evaluative (6-month trial outcomes); the NPV is a projection of long-run gains
studies.headlineVerbatim: The estimated cost of delivering the programme was €1463 per parent/ child. Further analysis indicated that, overall, it would cost €2304 to bring the average child in the study to below the clinical cut-off point for serious behavioural problems
otherFiguresVerbatim: we estimate the net present value of the IYP programme, (ie the return over and above the initial cost outlay and taking into account the fact that many of the gains may not be realised until some time in the future), to be approximately €4,599 per child.
cost €7,848 to bring the child with the highest intensity score to below the clinical cut-off for serious behavioural problems
studies.period: six-month outcomes; long-run gains projected using Irish data
outcomesValued: ECBI intensity score below clinical cut-off
studies.financialProxies: programme delivery costs; health and welfare service use; long-run gains 'valued using Irish data' (not detailed in the summary report)
studies.deadweight: not applicable - RCT (2:1 allocation, waiting-list control)
studies.dropOff: discounting implied in NPV; rate not stated in the summary report
studies.assurance: independent academic team; report prepared for the delivery organisation
studies.notes: No ratio given. The peer-reviewed economic paper is O'Neill et al. 2013 (separate entry). Search snippets quoting 'an economic rate of return of 11%' and '£1612-£2418 per child' were NOT verified in an opened source.

studies.title: A cost-effectiveness analysis of the Incredible Years parenting programme in reducing childhood health inequalities
studies.author: O'Neill D, McGilloway S, Donnelly M, Bywater T, Kelly P
studies.commissioner: not stated in abstract (economic component of the Incredible Years Ireland Study)
studies.journal: The European Journal of Health Economics 14(1)
studies.scope: Ireland - comparable programme that also runs in NI
studies.forecastOrEvaluation: evaluation, plus a qualitative consideration of long-run benefits
studies.headlineVerbatim: Our results show that the programme provides a cost-effective way of reducing behavioural problems. Furthermore, our cost analysis, when combined with a consideration of the potential long-run benefits, suggests that investment in such programmes may generate favourable long-run economic returns.
studies.financialProxies: not available - only the abstract was opened (full text paywalled)
studies.notes: Abstract only (via Europe PMC). No figures recorded because none appear in the abstract.

studies.title: Community Safety Initiatives Demonstrate Impressive Social Return on Investment (news item; underlying SROI report not found)
studies.author: Anita Doonan, Funding and Social Value Officer, Supporting Communities
studies.commissioner: Projects funded by the Northern Ireland Housing Executive (NIHE); analysis by Supporting Communities
studies.programme: YZone Youth Initiative, Portadown Elim Church (work with young people 'at-risk' or 'marginalised'); the same item reports Lisburn SAFE and Upper Springfield Development Trust community safety projects, which are not children-specific

studies.headlineVerbatim: The YZone Youth Initiative, run by Portadown Elim Church under the leadership of Campbell Best, has achieved an impressive SROI of £3.26 for every £1 invested.
otherFiguresVerbatim: The Resurgam Trust's Lisburn SAFE project has shown a social return on investment (SROI) of £3.03 for every £1 invested.
The Upper Springfield Development Trust's Community Safety Initiative in West Belfast ... has demonstrated the highest SROI of the three projects at £3.40 for every £1 invested.

studies.title: The Economic Value of Youth Work: A Report for UK Youth
studies.author: Frontier Economics
studies.programme: Youth work sector (incl. uniformed organisations, VCS, local authority provision)
studies.scope: UK national comparator (England); no NI figures
studies.method: economic value / return on investment model (fiscal and social savings, cost-benefit style); not SROI
studies.headlineVerbatim: results in an estimated return on investment (ROI) range of 3.2x to 6.4x, for the central benefits estimate. This means that for every pound the government invests in the youth sector, this generates between £3.20 and £6.40 in benefits to the taxpayer.
studies.ratioVerbatim: 3.2x to 6.4x (central); "a minimum of 2.5x and a maximum of 7.8x"
otherFiguresVerbatim: We estimate the total indirect value of the youth work sector to be £3.2bn, divided across: • £0.5bn from decreased crime • £1.7bn from improved health • £0.8bn from increased employment and education.
Excluding multipliers, we estimate total (labour and non-labour) expenditure in the sector to be £2.0bn.
studies.financialProxies: national data e.g. Understanding Society (36% of young people engaging), MoJ knife-crime data; Green Book 3.5% discount rate
studies.deadweight: not framed as deadweight; low/central/high assumptions on outcomes attributable to youth work
studies.attribution: low/central/high assumption ranges (e.g. proportion of knife crime caused by young people 41/55/69%)
studies.ownCommissioned: commissioned by UK Youth, a sector body
studies.notes: The report cites YouthLink Scotland (2016): "a return of £7 for every £1 of public expenditure" in Scotland. That study was not opened.

studies.title: Assessment of the Economic Value of Youth Work
studies.author: Indecon
studies.programme: Youth work sector, Exchequer-funded youth programmes
studies.headlineVerbatim: an overall net economic return arising from these quantified aspects of youth work of €1.21 billion, or a Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR) of 2.22:1
studies.deadweight: counterfactual assumptions on 'what would be the likely outcomes for individuals in the absence of the youth programmes'; sensitivity analysis run
studies.dropOff: discounted to present value; rate not extracted
studies.ownCommissioned: commissioned by NYCI, the sector representative body
studies.notes: Often quoted as '€2.20 for every €1'; the report's own wording is BCR 2.22:1.

studies.title: The short- and medium-term effects of Sure Start on children's outcomes
studies.author: Pedro Carneiro, Sarah Cattan, Gabriella Conti, Claire Crawford, Christine Farquharson, Nick Ridpath (Institute for Fiscal Studies)
studies.scope: UK national comparator for Sure Start NI (a different model; the NI programme is mentioned only in the policy implications)
studies.method: cost-benefit analysis based on quasi-experimental effect estimates
studies.forecastOrEvaluation: evaluation of observed effects plus projected lifetime earnings and tax effects
studies.headlineVerbatim: for every £1 the government spent on Sure Start centres, there were societal benefits of £2.05.
otherFiguresVerbatim: for every £1 of net spending, Sure Start may eventually generate around £11 in benefits for the children who attended.

if the actual impact on earnings and taxes were 10% lower than we estimate here, for example, this marginal value of public funds measure would fall to a ratio of £6.09 return for every £1 of net spending.
Up-front cost of Sure Start per cohort £2,690m ... Increased long-run tax revenues £1,860m
studies.period: one cohort of children in 2010 at programme peak, across five years of eligibility; 2023-24 prices
studies.financialProxies: cause-specific hospital costs; a month in care around £4,700 (2023-24 prices); court and offender management costs
studies.deadweight: not SROI terms; effects estimated against comparison areas (quasi-experimental)
studies.notes: Report notes 'the ratio of costs to benefits in earlier years should not necessarily be assumed to be the same'. NIAO (2026) records DE citing this English study for NI Sure Start.

studies.title: Costs and consequences of the Family Nurse Partnership (FNP) programme in England: evidence from the Building Blocks trial

studies.title: Managing children who offend (NIAO report; media release read)

studies.programme: Youth Justice Agency interventions, youth conferencing, Juvenile Justice Centre
studies.method: value-for-money audit (cost information; no cost-benefit performed)
studies.headlineVerbatim: The Department and the Youth Justice Agency lack the capacity to identify and apportion costs to the full range of interventions. The average cost per occupant each year in the JJC is £324,000.
